title: Capacitance sensing in bilayer graphene with gate reflectometry
authors: Tamás Kalmár, Gergő Fülöp, Bálint Szentpéteri, Olivér Kürtössy, Kenji Watanabe, Takashi Taniguchi, Szabolcs Csonka, Péter Makk
abstract: In the search for topological states in bilayer graphene, capacitance measurement methods are widely utilized in bridge type readouts or source-drain reflectometry setups. In this paper we demonstrate an alternative readout method based on gate reflectometry. We probe the capacitance of a BLG flake encapsulated between hBN and WSe$_2$ through a lumped-element LC resonator coupled to the top gate electrode of the heterostructure. The microwave readout reliably tracks the opening of a displacement field-induced band gap in the device. Compared to simultaneous DC transport measurements, the RF signal proves to be less affected by the percolating transport channels caused by sample disorder. Furthermore, we use the gate based readout to identify a small-angle alignment between the hBN and BLG flake. From the fixed frequency microwave readout, we extract the device capacitance change between the insulating and metallic state of the bilayer and utilize a comprehensive capacitance network model to explain its origin. Finally, we propose an advanced, multiplexed double-resonator readout scheme capable of simultaneously measuring top and bottom gate capacitances to extract the layer polarizability of the system. This work establishes gate reflectometry as a highly scalable and powerful methodology for exploring topological phases and internal charge dynamics in van der Waals heterostructures.
summary: This work introduces gate reflectometry as a superior technique for characterizing topological phases in bilayer graphene heterostructures. By coupling the device to an LC resonator, the authors can reliably measure capacitance changes associated with band gap opening, even in the presence of sample disorder. Furthermore, they extend this method to quantify the system's layer polarizability, opening new avenues for studying internal charge dynamics in 2D materials.
main_problem: To develop and demonstrate a novel, scalable, and powerful readout methodology to explore topological phases and internal charge dynamics in van der Waals heterostructures.
main_result: Gate reflectometry reliably tracks the opening of a displacement field-induced band gap, and the method allows for the extraction of layer polarizability by measuring top and bottom gate capacitances.
method: The study uses microwave reflectometry (measuring the reflection coefficient $S_{11}$) via a lumped-element LC resonator coupled to the top gate electrode, providing an alternative to standard DC transport measurements.
model_or_system: The system is bilayer graphene (BLG) encapsulated between hBN and WSe2, probed in a dual-gated setup. The analysis models the device capacitance using an effective parallel RC circuit and extends to a full capacitance network incorporating geometric and quantum compressibility corrections.
key_observables: Resonance frequency shift ($\delta f_0$), extracted device capacitance ($C_d$), layer polarizability ($\Pi$), and layer polarization ($P$).
important_parameters: Low temperatures (30 mK), displacement field ($D$), carrier density ($n$), and gate voltages.
main_assumptions: The analysis sometimes neglects large-value grounding capacitors ($C_{GND}$) and relies on approximations when deriving layer polarizability from the full capacitance matrix.
figures_summary: Figures show band structures for insulator/metallic phases, resonance curves demonstrating frequency shifts, and capacitance/polarizability maps showing tunability with gate voltages.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from demonstrating the basic measurement capability (tracking band gaps via RF signal) to detailed circuit modeling, and finally to deriving complex quantities like layer polarizability using advanced capacitance network theory.
why_interesting: The use of RF reflectometry to probe internal charge dynamics and topological gaps in 2D materials is a powerful, non-contact technique applicable to systems studied in AMO physics, such as superconducting qubits or quantum dots.
